content: Inhaled beclomethasone dipropionate (BDP), alongside inhaled budesonide, has been a cornerstone of anti-inflammatory treatment for asthma for many years. Recently, new prophylactic therapies for asthma have emerged, and BDP has been reformulated with a hydrofluoroalkane-134a (HFA) propellant, which is free of chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs). The purpose of this review was to compare the effectiveness of BDP with placebo, using both CFC and HFA propellants, in the treatment of chronic asthma. Additionally, the review aimed to investigate whether a dose-response relationship exists for BDP in asthma management and to establish a benchmark for evaluating newer asthma therapies. The review included randomized, parallel-group trials lasting at least four weeks, involving both children and adults. These trials compared CFC-BDP or HFA-BDP with placebo in the treatment of chronic asthma. A total of 60 studies, involving 6,542 participants, met the inclusion criteria. For CFC-BDP (57 studies), in patients not treated with oral steroids, doses of 400 mcg/day or less resulted in significant improvements in several measures of lung function compared to placebo. These included an increase in forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) by 360 mL (95% CI 260 to 460), an improvement in FEV1 as a percentage of predicted values by 12.41% (95% CI 8.18 to 16.64), and an increase in morning peak expiratory flow rate (am PEF) by 35.95 L/min (95% CI 27.85 to 44.04). Additionally, CFC-BDP reduced the use of rescue beta-2 agonists by 2.32 puffs/day (95% CI -2.55 to -2.09) and decreased the relative risk of trial withdrawal due to asthma exacerbations (RR 0.25, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.51). Subgroup analyses suggested that treatment durations longer than four weeks were necessary to achieve the full therapeutic effect. In patients treated with oral steroids, CFC-BDP significantly reduced oral prednisolone use by 4.91 mg/day (95% CI -5.88 to -3.94) and increased the likelihood of discontinuing oral steroid therapy (RR 8.02, 95% CI 3.23 to 19.92). For HFA-BDP (3 studies), in patients not treated with oral steroids, the drug was significantly more effective than placebo in improving FEV1, morning and evening PEF, and forced expiratory flow at 25-75% of the pulmonary volume (FEF25-75%). It also reduced asthma symptoms and daily beta-2 agonist use. These effects were evident after six weeks of treatment. In patients treated with oral steroids, HFA-BDP significantly improved FEV1 and morning PEF. However, there was considerable variability in the results, likely due to differences in study designs and objectives. Limited data were available on adverse events. The authors concluded that this review provides a quantitative assessment of the efficacy of both CFC-BDP and HFA-BDP in managing chronic asthma, strongly supporting their use. Current asthma guidelines recommend adjusting the dose based on individual patient response. However, the data do not support increasing the dose beyond 400 mcg/day in patients with mild to moderate asthma. There is insufficient evidence to determine a dose-response relationship in patients with severe asthma.
